basis: Cash basis, continuing operations, Group loan impairment expense (LIE). This line is identical between the cash and statutory income statements for both years (the $788m/$726m figures appear unchanged in the Consolidated (statutory) Income Statement, cross-referenced to the same Note 2.2), so there is no cash/statutory divergence to reconcile for this metric. The FY25 comparator ($726m) is the same figure CBA's own FY25 profit announcement reported at the time (no group-level restatement, though a small $2m segment-level reclassification exists — see disagreements).

loss_rate.unit: bps, annualised, loan impairment expense as a percentage of average gross loans and acceptances (GLAA) -- CBA's own denominator and computation, not independently recomputed (average GLAA is not disclosed as an absolute $ figure in these documents)

headline: CBA's Group loan impairment expense rose $62m (9%), from $726m in FY25 to $788m in FY26, and the loan loss rate rose 1bp, from 7bps to 8bps of average GLAA. CBA's own P&L reconciliation attributes the entire increase to a $150m rise in net collective provision funding, partly offset by a $17m fall in new/increased individual provisioning and a $71m larger write-back of individually assessed provisions (150 - 17 - 71 = 62, no residual). CBA's narrative names portfolio growth, increased geopolitical risk, macroeconomic uncertainty and (in Retail Banking Services) cost-of-living pressures as the causes of the collective-provisioning rise; these are not separately quantified in dollars.

drivers.name: Collective provisioning (net collective provision funding)
drivers.narrative: Net collective provision funding rose from $456m (FY25) to $606m (FY26), a $150m increase -- larger than the $62m net rise in total expense because it was partly offset by drivers 2 and 3 below. By segment, Retail Banking Services' LIE rose $106m to $378m and New Zealand's rose $11m to $66m, both citing higher collective provisions from geopolitical risk, macroeconomic uncertainty and (for New Zealand) a deteriorating unemployment outlook; Retail Banking Services also cites cost-of-living pressures. Business Banking and Institutional Banking and Markets also cite higher collective provisions from portfolio growth and macro/geopolitical risk, but each segment's overall LIE fell because larger offsetting reductions in individual provisioning/write-backs (drivers 2-3) outweighed this.

citations.quote: An increase in Retail Banking Services of $106 million to an expense of $378 million, primarily driven by increased geopolitical risk, macroeconomic uncertainty, and rising cost-of-living pressures
An increase in New Zealand of $11 million to an expense of $66 million, primarily driven by higher collective provisions reflecting deterioration in the unemployment outlook

drivers.name: New and increased individual (specific) provisioning
drivers.narrative: Gross new/increased individually assessed provisions fell slightly, from $439m (FY25) to $422m (FY26), a $17m reduction against the year's total expense increase. Business Banking (LIE -$45m to $310m) and Institutional Banking and Markets (LIE -$16m to $33m) both cite lower or released individually assessed provisions as a primary driver of their own LIE fall, while New Zealand cites higher individual provisioning as a partial offset to its collective-provision rise.

citations.quote: Net new and increased individual provisioning 422 439
A decrease in Institutional Banking and Markets of $16 million to an expense of $33 million, primarily driven by release of individually assessed provisions

drivers.name: Write-back of individually assessed provisions
drivers.narrative: Write-backs of individually assessed provisions grew from $169m (FY25) to $240m (FY26), a $71m larger reduction to expense. Business Banking explicitly names 'an increase in write-backs' among its drivers; the balance-sheet provisions note separately records that Corporate individually assessed provisions fell $6m, 'driven by write-backs and write-offs'.

citations.quote: A decrease in Business Banking of $45 million to an expense of $310 million, primarily driven by lower individually assessed provision charges, including an increase in write-backs
Corporate individually assessed provisions decreased $6 million or 1% to $694 million, driven by write-backs and write-offs

drivers.name: Portfolio growth (volume effect within collective provisioning)
drivers.narrative: Portfolio growth is repeatedly cited alongside macro/geopolitical risk as a driver of higher collective provisions (Business Banking, Institutional Banking and Markets, and Corporate collective provisions generally), consistent with gross loans and acceptances growing 7% to $1,087.6bn at 30 June 2026. CBA does not separately quantify a dollar volume component within the $150m collective-provisioning increase, so this is reported as unquantified.

citations.quote: partly offset by higher collective provisions reflecting portfolio growth, increased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty
Corporate collective provisions increased $172 million or 7% to $2,797 million, mainly reflecting portfolio growth, increased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty

drivers.name: Geopolitical risk, macroeconomic uncertainty, cost-of-living pressures and rising arrears
drivers.narrative: 'Increased geopolitical risk' and 'macroeconomic uncertainty' are cited in every segment's LIE commentary as a driver of the collective-provisioning increase; Retail Banking Services and the Group-level commentary also cite cost-of-living pressures and rising consumer arrears (home loan 90+ day arrears up to 0.73%, personal loan arrears up to 1.72%); New Zealand separately cites 'deterioration in the unemployment outlook'. None of these overlay/scenario effects are separately quantified in dollars in the source documents.

citations.quote: Loan impairment expense increased mainly reflecting portfolio growth, cost-of-living pressures and increased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty.
Home loan and personal loan arrears increased to 0.73% and 1.72% respectively reflecting cost-of-living pressures
Loan impairment expense (LIE) increased $62 million, with higher collective provisions mainly reflecting portfolio growth, increased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty

residual_note: The three quantified P&L-nature drivers sum exactly to the movement: +150 - 17 - 71 = 62 (CBA-FY26-profit-announcement.pdf, PDF p.118, Note 2.2). CBA's independent segment-level breakdown of the same $62m (Retail Banking Services +$106m, New Zealand +$11m, Corporate Centre and Other +$6m, Business Banking -$45m, Institutional Banking and Markets -$16m; PDF p.34) also sums exactly to $62m, cross-validating the movement from a second, non-overlapping disclosure lens (by segment rather than by provision type). The two lenses are not additive to each other -- each is a complete decomposition of the same $62m on its own terms.

disagreements.topic: FY25 segment split of loan impairment expense between Retail Banking Services and Business Banking
values: Retail Banking Services $272m / Business Banking $355m -- CBA-FY26-profit-announcement.pdf, PDF p.34 (FY25 shown as the restated comparative column)
Retail Banking Services $274m / Business Banking $353m -- CBA-FY25-profit-announcement.pdf, PDF p.34 (FY25 as originally reported)
disagreements.preferred: The FY26 profit announcement's restated split (RBS $272m / BB $355m), because the FY26 document is the basis for this task's driver decomposition and both documents footnote that 'comparative information has been restated to conform to presentation in the current period'. The $2m difference nets to zero at the Group level -- both documents report the FY25 Group total as $726m -- so it does not affect the movement, loss rate, or any of the quantified drivers above.
disagreements.explanation: A $2m reclassification between the Retail Banking Services and Business Banking segments occurred between the two disclosures, with no change to the Group total or to any figure used in this attribution's drivers (which are Group-level).

limitations: 'Net collective provision funding' ($150m) is a single group-level P&L reconciliation line (Note 2.2, PDF p.118). CBA does not split it into the canonical sub-drivers volume / asset-quality (risk migration) / forward-looking overlay in dollars, so those are reported unquantified (drivers 4-5) rather than estimated.

Average gross loans and acceptances (the loss-rate denominator) is not disclosed as an absolute dollar figure in any of the four source documents; only period-end GLAA ($1,087,560m at 30 Jun 26 vs $1,015,883m at 30 Jun 25) and CBA's own computed bps are given. The loss rate here is quoted directly from CBA, not independently recomputed.

New Zealand's loan impairment expense movement is reported in NZD in the results presentation (+NZD18m, PDF p.56) versus AUD in the profit announcement (+A$11m, PDF p.34); the AUD figure from the profit announcement is used above since that document is the primary group reconciliation source.

The results presentation (PDF p.24) states the FY26-vs-FY25 increase as '8.5%' versus the profit announcement's '9%' (PDF p.34, ASX announcement p.2); both derive from the identical $62m/$726m figures and differ only in rounding precision -- this is not treated as a disagreement.
Half-year (2H26 vs 1H26) driver detail exists in the same tables and was reviewed, but was not used in this attribution because the task's comparator is FY25 (full year), not 1H26.

Cash and statutory loan impairment expense were confirmed identical for both years by cross-referencing the Consolidated Income Statement (PDF p.88) to Note 2.2 (PDF p.118); no separate statutory-basis attribution was therefore required.
